lessons.title: Biggest, Smallest, Where
intro: You already know how to find the biggest value. Often you also want to know where it is. The trick: remember the position M instead of the value.
With the position, you get both: A(M) is the value, and M tells you where it sits in the list.
Searching works the same way: go through the list and stop as soon as you find what you're looking for.

exercises.prompt: Why does the example remember the position M instead of the value?
options: With the position, you know both the value A(M) and where it is
Values can't be stored in variables
exercises.explanation: A(M) gives the value at any time, so storing M is enough for both.

exercises.prompt: Change the search so it finds the smallest value instead.
exercises.explanation: Skip the update when A(I) is bigger or equal. M only moves when a smaller value comes along.
The search jumps out of the loop at the first 7 it finds, which is at position 3.

exercises.prompt: When 9 is missing, this prints NOT FOUND and then FOUND. After which line is a STOP missing?
exercises.explanation: After NOT FOUND, the program just continues with line 80. A STOP after line 70 ends it there.

exercises.prompt: How many values does a search through a list of 100 have to check in the worst case?
exercises.explanation: If the value is last or missing, every element has to be checked. That's called a linear search.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that prints the position of the biggest value, 2.
exercises.explanation: Fill the list, start with position 1, and move M whenever a bigger value shows up.

lessons.title: Bubble Sort
intro: Sorting means putting a list in order. Bubble sort is the simplest way: compare each pair of neighbors and swap them if they're in the wrong order.
One pass through the list moves the biggest value all the way to the end, like a bubble rising. Repeat the passes until everything is in order.
A list of N values needs at most N - 1 passes. And since the end of the list is already sorted after each pass, the inner loop can get shorter each time.

exercises.prompt: After the first pass of bubble sort, where is the biggest value?
options: At the end of the list
exercises.explanation: The biggest value wins every comparison, so it gets swapped forward until it reaches the end.

exercises.prompt: The list is 5, 3, 8, 1. What does it look like after the first pass?
exercises.explanation: 5 and 3 swap, 5 and 8 stay, 8 and 1 swap. The 8 has bubbled to the end.

exercises.prompt: How many passes does a list of 4 values need at most?
exercises.explanation: Each pass puts one more value in its final place. After 3 passes, the last one is automatically right too.

exercises.prompt: Sort from highest to lowest instead.
exercises.explanation: Now a pair is already in order when the first value is bigger or equal, so it's only swapped otherwise.

exercises.prompt: This swap loses a value. Which line is the problem?
exercises.explanation: Line 80 overwrites A(I) before it was saved. Like in Unit 5, a helper variable T is needed.

exercises.prompt: Why does the inner loop run only to 4 - P?
options: The values at the end are already sorted, so they don't need to be compared again
It's just a style choice and changes nothing
exercises.explanation: After pass P, the last P values are in place. Skipping them saves work.

lessons.title: Using a Sorted List
intro: Once a list is sorted, many questions become easy. The smallest value is first, the biggest is last.
The median, the value in the middle, is simply A(3) in a sorted list of 5. To show the top three, print the last three values backwards.
Equal values sit next to each other in a sorted list, so duplicates are easy to count by comparing neighbors.

exercises.prompt: In a sorted list of 5 values, which element is the median?
exercises.explanation: The median has as many values below it as above it: two on each side.

exercises.prompt: The list is sorted from small to big. How do you print the biggest value first?
exercises.explanation: FOR I = 5 TO 1 STEP -1 walks through the list from the end.

exercises.prompt: A is sorted: 2, 4, 7, 9. What does PRINT A(4) - A(1) show?
exercises.explanation: 9 - 2 = 7. This difference between biggest and smallest is called the range.

exercises.prompt: Print only the top three of a list sorted from high to low.
exercises.explanation: In a list sorted from high to low, the first three positions are the top three.

exercises.prompt: This counts equal neighbors, but stops with ?INDEX 6 OUT OF RANGE. Which line has to change?
exercises.explanation: For I = 5, line 40 looks at A(6), which doesn't exist. The loop must stop at 4.

exercises.prompt: Why sort the list before finding the median?
options: The median is only in the middle position once the list is in order
READ only works on sorted lists
exercises.explanation: In an unsorted list, the middle position can hold any value.
